title: Sentence Structure & Grammar
intro: You learn to find where a sentence starts and stops, to fix fragments, run-ons and comma splices, and to make subjects and verbs, pronouns and tenses agree. You use one routine for every editing question: S.C.A.N.

slides.h: Build a sentence that doesn't break

steps: **Find** the sentence: where does it start and stop?
**Spot** the broken ones: fragments, run-ons, comma splices.

list: **Editing questions:** drop-down lists inside the reading passages. Only one choice is correct.
**The essay:** one of the three scoring traits is clear, correct English.

reviewer.h: Why sentences matter on the GED

blocks.p: On the RLA test, grammar is tested with **drop-down** lists inside short texts like emails, letters and articles. You choose the version that is correct. In the essay, one of the three scoring traits is clear and correct English.

blocks.weak: I am writing about the supervisor job I saw your advert online I have four years of experience. Because I managed a team of nine people.
blocks.label: email
blocks.note: A run-on and a fragment make the writer look careless.

blocks.strong: I am writing about the supervisor job. I saw your advert online. I have four years of experience, and I managed a team of nine people.
blocks.label: email
blocks.note: The same facts, in clear sentences.

blocks.remember: Use **S.C.A.N.** for every editing question: Subject and verb · Complete · Agreement · Neat (punctuation).

blocks.p: A **clause** has a subject and a verb. An **independent clause** is a complete thought and can stand alone. A **dependent clause** starts with a waiting word and cannot stand alone.
Waiting words: **after, although, as, because, before, if, since, until, when, while**.

blocks.tip: If a group of words starts with a waiting word, look for the second half: *Because the bus arrived late, **I missed the meeting.***

blocks.p: A **fragment** is part of a sentence written as if it were complete. Use the 3-question test: Is there a subject? Is there a verb? Is the thought complete? If any answer is no, it is a fragment.

head: Fragment
What is missing
Fixed
rows: Ran to the station without a ticket.
**He** ran to the station without a ticket.
The manager and the whole night team.
The manager and the whole night team **worked late**.
Although the report was on time.
Although the report was on time, **the manager was not happy**.

blocks.mistake: Judging by length. "When the supervisor, who had worked at the plant for nineteen years, finally retired." is long but still a fragment. "She left." is short but complete.

blocks.p: A **run-on** joins two sentences with nothing. A **comma splice** joins two sentences with only a comma. Both are errors.

blocks.weak: The shop closed early we went home.
blocks.label: run-on

blocks.weak: The shop closed early, we went home.
blocks.label: comma splice

blocks.p: **The finger test:** cover the comma. Read the left side alone, then the right side alone. If both are complete sentences, a comma alone is not enough.

head: The four legal fixes
Example
rows: The shop closed early. We went home.
The shop closed early; we went home.
Comma + FANBOYS (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so)
The shop closed early, so we went home.
Because the shop closed early, we went home.

blocks.mistake: Fixing a comma splice with *however* and a comma: "It rained, however we played." *However* needs a semicolon or a period before it: "It rained; however, we played."

blocks.p: A singular subject takes a singular verb. A plural subject takes a plural verb. The GED often hides the subject behind extra words.

steps: Ask who or what does it. That is the real subject.
Cross out the words in the middle, especially after *of, with, along with, as well as, including*.
Read the subject and the verb alone.

blocks.strong: The collection of rare coins and stamps **is** in the east room.
blocks.label: sentence
blocks.note: One collection. "of rare coins and stamps" only describes it.

head: Rule
Example
rows: each, every, everyone, anyone, nobody, either, neither = singular
two subjects joined by and = plural
The manager and the clerk **are** here.
either…or / neither…nor: match the nearer subject
Neither the boxes nor the crate **fits**.
along with, as well as, together with change nothing
The teacher, along with her students, **was** late.
team, staff, committee, family = one group
there is / there are: the subject comes after the verb

blocks.p: A pronoun must match the word it replaces, and it must be clear. Ask two questions: **Who?** and **How many?**

head: Problem
Wrong
Right
rows: Give the file to Ahmed and I.
Give the file to Ahmed and **me**.
The report criticized the plan. This was unexpected.
The report criticized the plan. **This criticism** was unexpected.
The company changed their logo. (formal writing)

blocks.tip: For *Ahmed and I / me*, cover "Ahmed and". Give the file to **me**, not to *I*.

blocks.p: Stay in one time zone. Change the tense only when a time word gives a reason.

blocks.weak: She walked into the room and sits down.
blocks.label: sentence
blocks.note: Past, then present, for no reason.

blocks.strong: She walked into the room and sat down.
blocks.label: sentence

blocks.p: Items in a list should have the same form. A describing phrase must sit next to the word it describes.

glossary: clause
a group of words with a subject and a verb
independent clause
a clause that is a complete thought and can stand alone
dependent clause
a clause that starts with a waiting word and cannot stand alone
fragment
part of a sentence written as if it were complete
run-on
two sentences joined with no punctuation
comma splice
two sentences joined with only a comma
FANBOYS
for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so: joining words used with a comma
subject
who or what the sentence is about
verb
the action or state: what the subject does or is
agreement
matching singular with singular and plural with plural
pronoun
a word that replaces a noun: he, she, it, they, this
tense
the time of a verb: past, present or future
parallel structure
using the same form for items in a list
modifier
a word or phrase that describes something

workbook.q: Is each group of words a complete sentence or a fragment?
items: She left.
Because the shop was closed.
The workers finished the job.
Running to catch the bus.
workbook.why: "She left" and "The workers finished the job" have a subject, a verb and a complete thought. "Because…" needs a second half, and "Running…" has no subject and no main verb.

workbook.q: Choose the correct verb.
workbook.text: My brother {0} in a hotel. My sisters {1} at a bank.
workbook.why: "My brother" is one person, so the verb is "works". "My sisters" are more than one, so the verb is "work".

workbook.q: Which sentence is correct?
options: It was late we went home.
It was late, we went home.
It was late, so we went home.
It was late so, we went home.
workbook.why: C joins two sentences with a comma and "so" (FANBOYS). A is a run-on, B is a comma splice, and D puts the comma in the wrong place.

workbook.q: Choose the verb that keeps the same time.
workbook.text: Yesterday, I opened the door and {0} the lights on.
workbook.why: "Yesterday" and "opened" are in the past, so the second verb is also past: "turned".

workbook.q: Which sentence is correct?
options: Please send the report to Sara and I.
Please send the report to Sara and me.
Please send the report to me and Sara and I.
Please send the report to Sara and myself.
workbook.why: Cover "Sara and": send the report to **me**. "To I" is wrong, so "Sara and me" is correct.

workbook.q: "Although the meeting started late." How can you fix this fragment?
options: Although the meeting started late, we finished on time.
Although the meeting started late and.
workbook.why: "Although" is a waiting word, so the sentence needs a second half: "…, we finished on time."

workbook.q: Match each sentence with its fix.
items: The bus was full. We waited.
The bus was full; we waited.
The bus was full, so we waited.
Because the bus was full, we waited.
workbook.why: These are the four legal ways to fix "The bus was full, we waited." All four are correct.

workbook.q: Cross out the middle, then choose.
workbook.text: The box of old letters {0} in the cupboard. The list of names {1} on the wall.
workbook.why: The subjects are "the box" and "the list". Both are singular. "Of old letters" and "of names" only describe them.

workbook.q: Choose the correct verbs.
workbook.text: Everyone in the class {0} a laptop. The team {1} every Monday.
workbook.why: "Everyone" is singular, so it takes "has". "The team" is one group, so it takes "meets".

workbook.q: Add the missing subject. Type one word.
workbook.text: {0} ran to the station without a ticket.
workbook.why: The fragment has a verb (ran) but no subject. Adding a subject like "He" makes a complete sentence.

workbook.q: Which is the best revision? "Many workers prefer flexible hours, they say it reduces stress."
options: Many workers prefer flexible hours they say it reduces stress.
Many workers prefer flexible hours; they say it reduces stress.
Many workers prefer flexible hours, and, they say it reduces stress.
Many workers prefer flexible hours, they say, it reduces stress.
workbook.why: The semicolon correctly joins two complete sentences. A is a run-on. C has an extra comma after "and". D does not fix the splice.

workbook.q: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Neither the manager nor the workers was ready.
Neither the manager nor the workers were ready.
Neither the manager or the workers were ready.
Neither the managers nor the worker were ready.
workbook.why: With neither…nor, the verb matches the nearer subject. "Workers" is plural, so "were" is correct. C uses "or" instead of "nor". In D, "worker" is singular, so it needs "was".

workbook.q: Choose the clearest and most correct words.
workbook.text: The company updated {0} website. The new design is easy to use, and {1} has more information for customers.
workbook.why: "The company" is one organization, so use "its" (no apostrophe). The new design is one thing, so "it" is correct.

workbook.q: Which sentence is parallel?
options: The job needs patience, being careful and to work hard.
The job needs patience, care and hard work.
The job needs to be patient, care and working hard.
The job needs patience, careful and hard working.
workbook.why: In B, all three items are nouns: patience, care, hard work. The other choices mix different forms.

workbook.q: Which sentence is correct?
options: Walking to work, the rain started.
Walking to work, I felt the rain start.
The rain started walking to work.
Walking to work, it started to rain on me.
workbook.why: The phrase "Walking to work" must describe the person who walked. In B, "I" comes right after it. In A, the rain is walking.

workbook.q: Read the email. Choose the best option for each blank.
workbook.text:
Dear Ms. Alvarez,

I am writing about the warehouse supervisor position{0} I saw your advertisement online. I have four years of experience{1} and I managed a team of nine people. The list of my references {2} attached. My last two managers, along with my team leader, {3} happy to speak with you.
workbook.why: 1) Two sentences need a period. 2) Two complete sentences joined with "and" take a comma. 3) The subject is "the list" (one), so "is". 4) The subject is "my last two managers" (plural); "along with" changes nothing, so "are".

workbook.q: Tap the fragment.
sentences: The new clinic opened in March.
It has six doctors and a small pharmacy.
Because many families in the area had no clinic nearby.
Now most patients can see a doctor on the same day.
workbook.why: Sentence 3 starts with the waiting word "Because" and has no second half. It should be joined to sentence 1: "The new clinic opened in March because…"

workbook.q: Tap the sentence with an unnecessary tense change.
sentences: Last year, our company moved to a new office.
The building had more light and more space.
Staff members arrive earlier and stayed later.
Productivity rose by ten percent.
workbook.why: The paragraph is in the past (last year, moved, had, rose). "Arrive" is present. It should be "arrived".

workbook.q: Which is the best revision? "The report was finished on time, however the manager asked for changes."
options: The report was finished on time, however, the manager asked for changes.
The report was finished on time; however, the manager asked for changes.
The report was finished on time however the manager asked for changes.
The report was finished on time, however; the manager asked for changes.
workbook.why: "However" is not a FANBOYS word, so it cannot join two sentences with a comma. Use a semicolon before it and a comma after it.

workbook.q: Choose the correct verbs.
workbook.text: There {0} three reasons for the delay. The quality of the new machines {1} better than expected.
workbook.why: With "there is / there are", the subject comes after the verb: "three reasons" is plural, so "are". The subject of the second sentence is "the quality" (one), so "is".

checklist: use S.C.A.N. on an editing question
tell an independent clause from a dependent clause
find and fix a fragment with the 3-question test
find a run-on or comma splice with the finger test
fix a run-on four ways: period, semicolon, comma + FANBOYS, waiting word
make subjects and verbs agree, even when the subject is hidden
use pronouns that are clear and correct
make lists parallel and put describing phrases in the right place
